newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila urges caution on Spratly airstrip plan.
newsitem.headline: Manila urges caution on Spratly airstrip plan.

text.p: The Philippine Foreign Office on Friday urged caution on a plan by the military to set up aircraft refueling facilities on one of the disputed Spratly Islands.

Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said developing a recently renovated airstrip in the Kalayaan islands into a refuelling facility was a serious matter that needed consultation with other claimants to the Spratlys.

Armed forces chief General Arnulfo Acedera said on Thursday that the renovated airstrip, which he inaugurated on Christmas Day, could be a refuelling point for flights westward from the Philippines, to Vietnam and beyond.
He said the Philippines and Vietnam could jointly use the facility but added: "They (the Chinese) can use it as well."

The Spratlys are a cluster of potentially oil-rich but largely uninhabited isles, shoals and reefs in the South China Sea, and are claimed wholly or in part by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
Siazon said Manila had signed a code of conduct with some of the claimants intended to preserve the peace in the disputed area "and the first rule is no surprises."
"If it is a viable project, then we start consulting with our neighbours. We don't want surprises," Siazon told reporters.
"This is not a government position...All I'm saying is that the chief of staff may be thinking aloud," he said.
China's ambassador to the Philippines, Guan Dengming, said on Friday his government would not oppose the plan announced by Acedera.

"We have not received any formal proposal from the Philippine side but as the final purpose of such a possible station (is) for the service of all the concerned countries ... we are not opposed to such a goodwill suggestion," Guan told reporters.
But Guan, speaking through an interpreter, added: "We are opposed to any multilateral arrangement."
A Chinese embassy spokesman last week criticised the reopening of the Kalayaan airstrip and urged Manila not to take any action that would harm bilateral relations.
Acedera also said the Philippines planned to build a lighthouse on Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea, near the disputed Spratly Islands, to help ensure safety of navigation in the area.
He said in an interview with local reporters earlier this week that the lighthouse was necessary because 300 ships pass through the Scarbororough Shoal daily, making it "very dangerous" for shipping.
"There might be a collision," he said, according to a transcript of the interview obtained by Reuters on Friday.

Acedera said the Scarborough Shoal, about 200 nautical miles west of the Zambales coast in the northern Philippines, was not part of the disputed Spratly Islands and had been used by the Philippine air force in the past as a "live-fire" area.
"That is not a disputed area," he said.
